chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurara, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who was killed, and he had a brother in the House of Migration (who had migrated) and a brother in the House of the Bedouins (who had not migrated). I said: 'Do you see, if the emigrant forgives and the Bedouin wants to kill, is that for him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not for the Bedouin that he kills an emigrant until he emigrates.' I said: 'And if the emigrant forgives, then his forgiveness is valid.' I said: 'So is there for the Bedouin anything from the inheritance?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'As for the inheritance, he has his share from the wergild (blood money) of his brother, if it is taken.'

key_terms.دَارُ الْبَدْوِ: House of the Bedouins (referring to those who have not migrated)
key_terms.دَارُ الْهِجْرَةِ: House of Migration (referring to those who have performed hijrah)
key_terms.عَفَا: To forgive (in the context of qisas/retaliation)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on retaliation and inheritance when one brother has migrated and the other has not?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the juristic distinction between the right of retaliation (qisas) and inheritance (mirath) among brothers of differing migration statuses, a key topic in early Shia fiqh regarding the social hierarchy of the Muhajirun. It clarifies that while the non-migrating brother retains a share of the wergild (diyah) upon forgiveness, his right to execute the killing is contingent upon his own migration, reflecting the spiritual and legal precedence of the Hijrah. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly view that migration is not merely geographical but a condition for full legal agency in blood-kinship matters.

en.hubeali: Ibn Mahboub, from Ali Bin Raib, from Zurara who said,

‘I asked Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> about a man who was killed, and for him is a brother in the house of the migration, and for him is a brother in the house of the Bedouins who did not migrate. What is your<sup>asws</sup> view if the emigrant forgive and the Bedouin want that he be killed. Is that for him (to do)? It is not for the Bedouin that he kills an emigrant until he emigrates’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If the emigrant forgives, so his forgiveness is allowed’. I said, ‘So is there for the Bedouin anything from the inheritance?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘As for the inheritance, so for him is his share from the wergild of his brother, if he takes it’.
